item.title: Concerns raised over medical team’s sea travel
item.description: A VETERAN seafarer has questioned why frontline medical teams are still being transported in small fibreglass boats decades after government-operated medical vessels once served Fiji’s maritime communities. Operations manager of the inter-island passenger vessel MV Yavirau, Raivolita Uluilakeba raised the concerns in a social media post while reacting to the disappearance of six Ministry of Health
item.content:encoded:
A VETERAN seafarer has questioned why frontline medical teams are still being transported in small fibreglass boats decades after government-operated medical vessels once served Fiji’s maritime communities.

Operations manager of the inter-island passenger vessel MV Yavirau, Raivolita Uluilakeba raised the concerns in a social media post while reacting to the disappearance of six Ministry of Health officials in Lau waters on Wednesday.

The six healthcare workers went missing while travelling by boat on an official outreach mission, prompting a major multi-agency search and rescue operation.

Reflecting on his years with the former Fiji Marine Department in the 1980s, Mr Uluilakeba said medical ships were once strategically stationed across the country to transport medical teams and respond to emergencies.

“Just resting on MV Yavirau at Lakeba, and gazing out to sea with silent hopes for the missing,” Mr Uluilakeba wrote.

“Thinking back, to those days in the Fiji Marines, mid 80s, where I began my seafaring career, the Fiji Marine Department (now GSS) had medical ships stationed around the country, all manned by Fiji Marine Government crew.

“We had MV Vuniwai ni Lau stationed in Lakeba and another stationed in Vanuabalavu, at Levuka we had the Cagi mai Ra.

Mr Uluilakeba said the vessels were specifically designed to support healthcare delivery to Fiji’s maritime islands.

“Their main purpose ??…we’re to standby for medical emergencies and transport medical staff on their frequent tours to their districts.

“These ships could transfer patients, had showers, galley and comfortable beds for medical staff.”

Questioning the current state of maritime health transport, he wrote:

“So here we are decades forward, and our medical staff are still being transported in fibreglass boats.

“Did bringing in a moving eight (8) million dollar hospital ship, MV Veivueti solve the problem?”

item.title: A new era for care
item.description: THE Government has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening childhood cancer care, with a $41million investment in Fiji’s first Radiotherapy and Cancer Treatment Centre and continued support for families battling the disease. Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa made the announcement yesterday while speaking at the launch of Childhood Cancer Awareness Month, saying improving outcomes f
item.content:encoded:
THE Government has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening childhood cancer care, with a $41million investment in Fiji’s first Radiotherapy and Cancer Treatment Centre and continued support for families battling the disease.

Assistant Minister for Health Penioni Ravunawa made the announcement yesterday while speaking at the launch of Childhood Cancer Awareness Month, saying improving outcomes for young patients required a stronger and more resilient health system.

“The ministry remains committed to strengthening early diagnosis, improving referral pathways, expanding specialist services and ensuring children have access to quality treatment regardless of where they live,” he said.

“Reliable information is equally important.

“Strengthening cancer registration and data collection enables us to better understand disease patterns, plan services effectively and continue improving patient outcomes.”

Mr Ravunawa said Government remained committed to improving cancer care through increased investment and partnerships.

“We are proud to support WOWS Kids Fiji through a $100,000 Government grant, assisting the organisation to continue delivering practical support to children and families across Fiji.

“In addition, the 2026–2027 National Budget includes $41million towards establishing Fiji’s first Radiotherapy and Cancer Treatment Centre.

“This represents one of the most significant investments in cancer care in our nation’s history.

“For many families, it will mean improved access to specialised treatment closer to home and reduced financial and emotional hardship.”

He said Government could not tackle childhood cancer alone, stressing that success depended on partnerships with organisations such as WOWS Kids Fiji, healthcare professionals, communities, churches, schools, businesses and development partners.

item.title: Munia regains land title
item.description: AFTER 36 years, the Yavusa Munia has regained ownership of its 1110-hectare land on Avea Island in Vanuabalavu, Lau, following its acquisition under the Government’s Freehold Land Buyback Scheme. The historic handover of the original freehold title was marked by the sound of traditional drums as members of the yavusa gathered to celebrate the return of their ancestral land.
item.content:encoded:
AFTER 36 years, the Yavusa Munia has regained ownership of its 1110-hectare land on Avea Island in Vanuabalavu, Lau, following its acquisition under the Government’s Freehold Land Buyback Scheme.

The historic handover of the original freehold title was marked by the sound of traditional drums as members of the yavusa gathered to celebrate the return of their ancestral land.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka officiated at the ceremony on Wednesday and described the occasion as the beginning of a new chapter for the landowners.

Speaking in the iTaukei language, Mr Rabuka said the return of the island represented more than the restoration of ownership, but the return of identity, hope and responsibility.

He called on landowners to protect the island’s natural environment, saying economic development and environmental conservation must go hand in hand. For the people of Munia, the ceremony closed a painful chapter in their history.

Speaking on behalf of the villagers, 70-year-old Etuate Uni said the day would be remembered for generations.

He said their forefathers endured great hardship after being forced to leave Munia.

“What we are witnessing today is the reality of what our forefathers dreamed and worked so hard for. This is proof that their struggles were not in vain,” Mr Uni said.

item.title: Mother shares emotional journey
item.description: MOTHER of triplets Akanisi Vulimaiigiladi was four months pregnant when she knew her life would not be the same. The Vunisei, Toga, Rewa native said she was told by doctors that two of her daughters were conjoined twins.
item.content:encoded:
MOTHER of triplets Akanisi Vulimaiigiladi was four months pregnant when she knew her life would not be the same.

The Vunisei, Toga, Rewa native said she was told by doctors that two of her daughters were conjoined twins.

“It came as a shock when we first got the news but we kept praying for God’s guidance,” said Mrs Vulimaiigiladi.

Late last year, Mrs Vulimaiigiladi welcomed the triplets Di Cecea, Jesipeli Kikau and Hossana.

From there on the young family had made countless visits and reviews from medical professionals working hard to help her conjoined twins Di Cecea and Jesipeli Kikau.

“From the moment they were born there were specialist doctors present.

“So we did not give up because people were willing to help us from the very beginning.”

That help came last week when the Mrs Vulimaiigiladi and husband Vakatale Vulimaiigiladi were informed they would be travelling to Saudi Arabia to the King Salman Hospital, where a multi-million dollar, life-changing separation surgery would be carried out for their daughters.

“The past few days has been a display of God’s and people’s kindness.

“We didn’t expect that so many people would reach out to us and offer support.

“I want to thank my family and my husband’s family for being here for us from the start and offering support for our journey to Saudi Arabia.”

The family left on a Fiji Airways flight to Hong Kong on July 29 from the Nadi International Airport where they will board a flight to Qatar before landing in King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

According to the Ministry of Health, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia has fully funded the entire trip, covering airfares and accommodation, with the surgery to be conducted free of charge under humanitarian grounds.

item.title: Mobile wallet probe
item.description: THE Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) says there are “a lot of red flags” surrounding Vodafone Fiji’s M-PAiSA auto-renew feature as it investigates complaints of money being deducted from customers’ e-wallets without clear notice. FCCC said that while there is no specific law governing auto-renewals, it is examining provisions relating to “unconscionable conduct” under the FCCC Act
item.content:encoded:
THE Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) says there are “a lot of red flags” surrounding Vodafone Fiji’s M-PAiSA auto-renew feature as it investigates complaints of money being deducted from customers’ e-wallets without clear notice.

FCCC said that while there is no specific law governing auto-renewals, it is examining provisions relating to “unconscionable conduct” under the FCCC Act.

“There have to be some standards,” FCCC chief executive officer Senikavika Jiuta said.

“There have to be disclosures. It has to be a reasonable time for the consumers to make that choice. And I see there are a lot of red flags with this issue.”

The commission said it is reviewing the matter and has advised customers who believe they were charged without their permission to lodge a formal complaint.

“For any consumer, the fact that your money is being deducted without your knowledge, it’s a breach of your privacy. You are not informed.

“The fact that you are touching other people’s e-wallets without the consent, to us that’s a concern.”

Ms Jiuta also raised concerns about transparency, saying “in the transaction history it’s not there as well”.

The complaints have reignited debate over automatic billing and consumer rights in Fiji, with numerous complaints continuing to surface on social media.

Henry Vesikula, 28, an M-PAiSA user from Nadi claimed he only got the text after the deduction.

“If we wanted to unsubscribe from the plan, we had to dial *181#, Option 3, Option 5, or go via the M-PAiSA App,” Mr Vesikula said.

“But banks don’t do that, and I don’t know why Vodafone is doing that.

“They have failed to consult customers with no explanation.

“It’s like them telling us indirectly, ‘If you want to unsubscribe, you can do it yourself, but if you don’t, we’ll do it on your behalf.’”

Vodafone Fiji defended the feature, saying it was introduced on June 10, 2026.

“The feature applies only to eligible self-subscribed plans and requires customer consent, including PIN authentication, at the time of purchase,” a Vodafone spokesperson said.

Vodafone said customers were notified of the renewal terms, they receive confirmation and reminder SMS messages, and they may disable the feature at any time by dialing *181#, Option 3, Option 5, or via the M-PAiSA App.

The company urged customers experiencing issues to call 123 or 124, visit a retail outlet, or contact its official social media team.

This assignment has now successfully c
item.content:encoded:
Publicly listed Sun Insurance Company Ltd (SPX:SUN) has cleared the air on its engagement with former Fijian Holdings Ltd chief executive officer Nouzab Fareed, who was recently found guilty of two counts of indecent assault.

“SUN had provided a consultancy assignment to Mohammed Nouzab Fareed, as chief transformational consultant, over a period of 20 months. This assignment has now successfully completed and concluded,” the general insurer said in a statement filed at the South Pacific Stock Exchange (SPX) on Tuesday.

“SUN wishes to clarify that the company is aware of the recent publicity regarding its consultant.

“The company is aware that the matter relates to Mr Fareed’s previous employment and acknowledges the court’s decision. The matter does not relate to Sun Insurance Company Ltd’s operations, financial reporting or its customers.

“The board would like to acknowledge Mr Fareed for his sterling work in carrying out the objectives set for him within the confined period.”

Mr Fareed was appointed chief transformation officer for SUN last year.

item.title: Citizens budget to enhance transparency and understanding
item.description: Every Fijian regardless of their language or background will now be able to better understand the 2026-27 National Budget after the launch of the Citizens’ Guide to the National Budget in English, Hindi and iTaukei. During the launch at the Ministry of Finance office in Suva on Wednesday, Minister for Finance Esrom Immanuel said the Citizens’ Budget will enhance transparency and accountability.
item.content:encoded:
Every Fijian regardless of their language or background will now be able to better understand the 2026-27 National Budget after the launch of the Citizens’ Guide to the National Budget in English, Hindi and iTaukei.

During the launch at the Ministry of Finance office in Suva on Wednesday, Minister for Finance Esrom Immanuel said the Citizens’ Budget will enhance transparency and accountability.

He said publishing the Citizens’ Budget in three main languages will enable every citizen to understand the government’s priorities and appreciate how public resources are being invested to improve their lives.

“The Citizens’ Budget distils key information into a concise and reader-friendly 20-page publication,” Mr Immanuel said.

“It outlines the government’s revenue and expenditure plans, major policy priorities in infrastructure, health, education and social protection and the key economic forecast as well as the medium-term fiscal strategy,” he said.

Mr Immanuel said the 2026-27 national budget was formulated during a period of considerable economic uncertainty.

“The global fuel and energy crisis that placed significant pressure on the economy, public finances and the cost of living, requiring the government to make careful and responsible policy choices.

“At the same time, government had to make provision for several major national priorities that could not be deferred including funding for the general election, constitutional referendum, the national census and the commencement of major capital projects that are critical to Fiji’s long-term development and future prosperity,” he said.

“This reflects a disciplined and balanced fiscal approach, one that continues to invest in Fiji’s long-term development while safeguarding fiscal sustainability,” he said.

He said the government has looked at the welfare of the people and the economy to ensure the economy keeps functioning despite the crisis faced.

item.title: Optimism for higher growth
item.description: Government has defended the economic growth of 1.5 per cent as forecasted in the 2026-27 National Budget, saying it was prepared based on a worst-case scenario considering the geopolitical issues affecting the country. Following the ANZ’s Pacific Insight Report in which ANZ’s senior Pacific economist Dr Kishti Sen highlighted that the local economic growth would outpace the budgeted forecast, Mini
item.content:encoded:
Government has defended the economic growth of 1.5 per cent as forecasted in the 2026-27 National Budget, saying it was prepared based on a worst-case scenario considering the geopolitical issues affecting the country.

Following the ANZ’s Pacific Insight Report in which ANZ’s senior Pacific economist Dr Kishti Sen highlighted that the local economic growth would outpace the budgeted forecast, Minister for Finance Esrom Immanuel said the economic growth will be better than what had been forecasted in the budget.

“It will be better than what we budgeted, because we prepared this budget on a worst-case scenario, projecting that this fuel crisis and the effect of it or the ramification of it will go on for another six or nine months,” Mr Immanuel said.

“As you can see in the global news that the war is still happening. So, it will go on for some time. But we believe that we can do and we’ll do better based on ANZ’s projections,” he said.

Mr Immanuel said if the economic performance exceeds expectations and generates a surplus, then the additional funds would be used in key priority areas.

“Any surplus will probably be used in three areas—for future needs, reducing government debt, and supporting other important priorities, whether that is infrastructure development or other sectors that require assistance,” he said.

Meanwhile, in the ANZ Pacific Insight Report, Dr Sen has projected that Fiji’s 2026 economic growth will outpace the Government’s 1.5 per cent “worst-case” budget projection.

He said they are forecasting real gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 2.7 per cent this year and 2027, driven by record remittances, tourism and rising agricultural exports.

In a similar report released earlier this month, Dr Sen said the national budget had assumed a worst-case set of economic assumptions to project revenue.
